posts.title: Is someone already inside your phone?
posts.listDesc: The 5-minute check that tells you for sure — session lists, unknown devices, and what to do if you find something.
posts.intro: Right now, on the exact phone in your hand, there could be a device logged into your account that isn't yours. Maybe there isn't — but you don't actually know, because most people never check. This is the real 5-minute check, not a hypothetical: no app to install, nothing to buy, just open a settings menu and look.
posts.tldr: Check which devices are signed into your Apple ID or Google account. Scan your app list for anything you don't recognize. And look for configuration profiles or device admin apps you never set up — that last one's the one people usually skip, and it's the one worth checking most. Five minutes, all built into your phone already.
posts.statLine: $ context — 292 days. That's the average time it takes someone to realize their login was stolen, according to IBM. Nearly a year of someone else quietly having access, before anyone notices.

sections.title: Check who's actually logged in

paragraphs: Open Settings → [your name] → Password Options → Security Recommendations, or just scroll down from Settings → [your name] — either way, you'll see the full list of every device currently signed into your Apple ID. Every single one.
Open the Google app → Profile picture → Manage your Google Account → Security → Your devices — this is the full guest list for your Google account, every device currently signed in.
Scan it slowly. A device model you've never owned. A city you've never set foot in. A login time you can't place. Any one of those is worth stopping on.

sections.title: Look for apps you didn't install

paragraphs: Scroll through your full app list — not just your home screen, the real list under Settings → Apps. Spyware doesn't usually announce itself; it likes boring, forgettable names like "System Update," "Device Health," or "Battery Optimizer" — huh, funny how none of those actually tell you anything.
If you can't remember installing something and can't explain what it does, don't shrug it off. That's exactly the gap it's counting on.

sections.title: Check for a profile you didn't set up

paragraphs: Go to Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. A configuration profile is normal on a work phone — someone in IT put it there on purpose. On your personal phone, one you don't remember installing means someone else may have remote access to it. That's not routine, that's a red flag.

Go to Settings → Security → Device admin apps. Anything sitting here you didn't knowingly turn on — an unfamiliar "Find My Device"-style app, say — deserves a second look before you move on. If you don't recognize it, don't just shrug and close the screen.

sections.title: Run your phone's built-in security checkup

paragraphs: Both Google and Apple already built the easy version of this for you — Google Account → Security → Security Checkup, or the Security Recommendations screen from Step 1 on iPhone. One tap. It flags weak passwords, reused passwords, sign-ins you don't recognize. You didn't even have to think about it.

quiz.question: Have you checked which devices are logged into your phone or accounts in the last 6 months?

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU FIND SOMETHING
warn.text: Don't panic, but do act. Sign out of any device you don't recognize, change your password from a device you trust — not the compromised one — and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already on. If it looks like stalkerware specifically, know that removing it may alert whoever installed it. If this is a safety concern involving another person, that's worth thinking through carefully before you act. Take your time with that part.

checklist: Checked which devices are logged into your Apple ID / Google account
Scanned your full app list for anything unfamiliar
Checked for configuration profiles / device admin apps you didn't set up
Ran the built-in security checkup

posts.title: The password mistake nobody thinks is a big deal
posts.listDesc: Why reusing one password anywhere is worse than you think, and how a password manager actually fixes it.
posts.intro: Here's the spoiler: it's reusing the same password on more than one site. It feels completely harmless — until it's the reason your email, your bank, and half your other accounts all get hit on the same afternoon.
posts.tldr: Run a password checkup and see what's reused or compromised — brace yourself, the list is usually longer than you think. Turn on your phone's built-in password manager. Fix email, banking, and payment-linked accounts first; the manager handles the rest as you go.
posts.statLine: $ context — one password, leaked from any random site you signed up for years ago, can unlock every other account where you reused it. It's called credential stuffing, and a machine does it in seconds, not a person.

sections.title: See if you've actually done this

paragraphs: Go to passwords.google.com or Settings → Password Manager → Password Checkup and let it do the uncomfortable part for you — it'll show you exactly which passwords are reused, weak, or already sitting in a known breach.
Go to Settings → Passwords → Security Recommendations. Same idea — it flags reused and compromised passwords for you automatically.
Most people are surprised by how long that list is. That's normal, not a sign you did anything unusually careless — this is just what everyone's list looks like before they check.

sections.title: Understand why this actually matters

bad.label: ✕ ONE PASSWORD, EVERYWHERE
bad.text: Say it's some newsletter you signed up for back in 2019 and never thought about again — that site gets breached. Your email and that password leak together. Within seconds, automated tools are trying that exact combo on your bank. Your real email. Your Instagram. Not because anyone's targeting you specifically — a machine doesn't care, it just tries the combo everywhere.

good.label: ✓ UNIQUE PER SITE
good.text: That same site gets breached. But the leaked password is useless anywhere else, because it was never used anywhere else. The damage stops at one account instead of spreading through your entire digital life.

sections.title: Set up a password manager (it's easier than remembering)

paragraphs: Good news — you don't have to memorize a unique password for every single account. (Nobody actually does that, whatever anyone tells you.) A password manager remembers them for you, and your phone almost certainly already has one built in, for free: iCloud Keychain if you're on iPhone, Google Password Manager if you're Android or Chrome.
Want one that works identically no matter what device or browser you're on? Bitwarden is free and widely trusted. Either path is a genuine upgrade over trying to remember it all yourself.

sections.title: Fix your most important accounts first

paragraphs: You don't need to fix every account today — that's how people give up halfway through. Start with the ones that would hurt most if compromised: your primary email (it can reset almost everything else), your banking apps, and anything with saved payment info.
Let the password manager generate a new, unique password for each one as you go, and just keep chipping away at the rest over time.

warn.label: ⚠ IF A PASSWORD SHOWS UP AS "COMPROMISED"
warn.text: Change it immediately, starting with that account and anywhere else you used the same one. If it's your email password specifically, treat it as urgent — email is usually the master key to everything else you own online.

checklist: Ran a password checkup to see what's reused or compromised
Turned on your phone's built-in password manager
Fixed email, banking, and payment-linked accounts first
Let the manager generate unique passwords going forward

posts.title: What is smishing?
posts.listDesc: The exact texts scammers send, why they work, and how to tell a real message from a fake one in seconds.
posts.intro: Smishing is just SMS phishing — a scam text engineered to look official enough that you click before your brain catches up. The wording changes every time. The pattern underneath almost never does, and once you can see it, these texts stop working on you.
posts.tldr: Scam texts always follow the same pattern. A trusted name. A fake urgent problem. A link. Never tap it — go to the official app or type the website yourself. That one habit alone defeats almost all of them.
posts.statLine: $ context — smishing works because a text feels more urgent and more "official" than an email ever does, and almost nobody's ever been taught to question one.

sections.title: The pattern, not the exact words

paragraphs: Almost every smishing text is built the same way. A name you trust — your bank, a delivery company, the tax office. A problem that supposedly needs fixing right now. A link that promises to fix it. Swap out the wording and it looks like a brand new scam. It isn't. It's the same three pieces, every time.

items.text: A package supposedly couldn't be delivered — click the link to pay a small fee or "confirm" your address.
Suspicious activity on your account, apparently — click through and "verify" by logging in on their page, not yours.
You've supposedly won something, and the countdown clock in the text wants you to "claim" it before you have time to think.

sections.title: Check the sender, not just the message

paragraphs: Real companies text from consistent, verifiable numbers or short codes — the same one, message after message. Scam texts tend to come from a random-looking mobile number, an email-style address, or a number that's different every single time.
When in doubt, scroll back to a past message from that company and compare. Does the number actually match?

sections.title: Never tap the link — go direct instead

paragraphs: Don't tap the link — not even just to look. Open the company's official app instead, or type in their website address yourself, from memory. If something's genuinely wrong with your account or your delivery, it'll be sitting right there too, no scam link required.

sections.title: Notice the urgency — it's the biggest tell

paragraphs: "Act now." "Your account will be suspended." "Offer expires in 1 hour." None of that's an accident. It's the scammer doing your thinking for you, on purpose, so you click before you catch up. Ask yourself: when's the last time your actual bank texted you an ultimatum with a countdown clock? Never. That's the tell.

quiz.question: When you get a text claiming there's a "delivery problem," what do you do?
quiz.safeLabel: Check the official app or site instead

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY CLICKED
warn.text: Don't enter anything if a page asks for a password, card number, or OTP — close it immediately. If you already entered something, change that password right away and check your bank/card statements for anything unfamiliar over the next few days.

checklist: Checked whether the sender number matches past legitimate messages
Didn't tap the link — went to the official app/site directly instead
Noticed the manufactured urgency for what it was
Knows what to do if a link was already tapped

posts.title: Incognito mode doesn't make you anonymous
posts.listDesc: It hides your history from the next person on this computer. It was never designed to hide you from anyone else.
posts.intro: Incognito (or "private") mode is one of the most misunderstood buttons in your browser. People treat it like an invisibility cloak. It's really just a note that says "don't remember this" — and only your own browser reads that note.
posts.tldr: Incognito mode only stops your browser from saving local history, cookies, and autofill. It does nothing to hide you from your Wi-Fi network, your employer or school, or the websites you actually visit — you're not anonymous, just forgetful on purpose.
posts.statLine: $ context — a 2018 Google-commissioned study found most people believe incognito mode hides their activity from their internet provider. It doesn't, and it never has.

sections.title: What incognito actually turns off

paragraphs: Incognito mode does exactly three things: it stops your browser from saving new history, it doesn't keep cookies after you close the window, and it doesn't save anything you type into forms. That's the whole feature.

It's genuinely useful for that — checking someone else's email on a shared laptop, or shopping for a gift without your browser suggesting it to the person you're buying it for. It was built to solve that problem, not the problem people think it solves.

sections.title: What it was never designed to hide

bad.label: What people think happens
bad.text: My internet provider, my Wi-Fi network, and the websites I visit have no idea it's me.

good.label: What actually happens
good.text: Your internet provider and network can still see every site you visit. The websites themselves can still see your IP address and fingerprint your device.

paragraphs: None of that visibility depends on cookies or saved history — it happens at the network and server level, which incognito mode never touches. If you're on a work or school network, whoever manages it can very likely still see exactly what you looked at.

sections.title: What actually gets you closer to private

paragraphs: A VPN hides your traffic from your network and ISP — that's a real privacy layer incognito mode isn't. A tracker-blocking browser cuts down on cross-site tracking. Neither makes you invisible, but both do something incognito mode structurally can't.
The Toolkit has free, open-source picks for both if you want to actually close this gap instead of assuming a button already closed it.

quiz.question: Before reading this, did you think incognito mode hid your browsing from your Wi-Fi network or ISP?
quiz.safeLabel: No, I knew it was local-only

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE BEEN RELYING ON IT
warn.text: If you've used incognito mode assuming it hid something sensitive from your network administrator or ISP, it didn't — that visibility was there the whole time. Going forward, a VPN is the tool that actually addresses that, not a browser mode.

checklist: Knows incognito mode only stops local history, cookies, and autofill from saving
Understands your ISP and network can still see every site visited
Knows websites can still see your IP address and device fingerprint
Has a real privacy tool (VPN) in mind for when that actually matters

posts.title: The AI phone call that sounds exactly like your kid
posts.listDesc: It only takes a few seconds of audio from a social media video to clone a voice convincingly enough to fool a parent.
posts.intro: "Mom, I'm in trouble, please don't tell Dad, I need money right now." The voice is shaking. It sounds exactly like your kid — because in a growing number of these calls, it's an AI clone built from a few seconds of their voice pulled off a public video.
posts.tldr: AI can clone a convincing voice from just a few seconds of audio, which is exactly what these fake emergency calls use. The defense isn't spotting a fake voice — it's hanging up and calling back on a number you already know, every single time.
posts.statLine: $ context — the FTC has warned that voice-cloning tools now need as little as 3 seconds of sample audio to produce a convincing clone, most of which people post publicly without a second thought.

sections.title: How the scam actually works

paragraphs: A scammer pulls a short clip of someone's voice — a public video, a voicemail greeting, a livestream — and feeds it into a voice-cloning tool. Minutes later, they can make that cloned voice say anything, in real time, over a phone call.

The call comes in from an unknown or spoofed number. The "kid" is crying, panicked, in some kind of trouble — a car accident, an arrest, a medical emergency — and needs money sent immediately, usually by wire transfer, gift cards, or crypto.

sections.title: The tells that give it away almost every time

items.text: You're pushed to act in minutes, with no time to think, verify, or call anyone else first.
The request is for wire transfer, gift cards, or crypto — never a normal, traceable, reversible payment method.
You're told not to tell another family member — a classic move to stop anyone from checking the story.
The audio is often slightly off — a bit robotic, oddly paced, or conveniently "breaking up" right when details would get specific.

sections.title: The one habit that defeats it

paragraphs: Hang up, and call that person back directly on a number you already have saved — not a number the caller gives you. If they're genuinely fine, you'll know in under a minute. If it was a scam, it ends right there.
Some families set up a private "safe word" nobody outside the family knows, to ask for on any call like this. It's a small thing, but a cloned voice can't guess a word it's never heard.

quiz.question: You get a call that sounds exactly like your kid, panicked, asking you to send money right now. What do you do?
quiz.safeLabel: Hang up and call them back directly

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY SENT MONEY
warn.text: Contact your bank or payment provider immediately — the faster you report it, the better the odds of stopping or reversing the transfer. Then file a report with the FTC (reportfraud.ftc.gov) so the pattern gets tracked.

checklist: Knows a convincing voice clone can be made from just a few seconds of audio
Recognizes the urgency + secrecy + untraceable-payment pattern
Has a habit of hanging up and calling back on a known number
Knows what to do if money was already sent

next.desc: The single biggest security upgrade you can make today, in under five minutes.

posts.title: Turn on 2FA — here's what it actually protects
posts.listDesc: A stolen password alone stops working the moment 2FA is on. It's the single biggest upgrade available to you, and it takes about five minutes.
posts.intro: Two-factor authentication (2FA) means proving it's you with something beyond just a password — a code, an app tap, or a physical key. If your password ever leaks in a breach, and eventually one will, 2FA is what stands between that leak and someone actually getting into your account.
posts.tldr: 2FA stops a stolen or leaked password from being enough to get into your account on its own. Turn it on for email first, then banking, then anything else — an authenticator app beats SMS codes, which can be intercepted.
posts.statLine: $ context — Microsoft has reported that accounts with any form of 2FA enabled block over 99% of automated account-takeover attempts, even when the password itself is already compromised.

sections.title: What 2FA actually stops

paragraphs: A password is one proof of identity — something you know. 2FA adds a second, different kind of proof — something you have (your phone, a security key) or something you are (a fingerprint). An attacker who steals your password from a breach still doesn't have the second piece.

This is exactly what stops credential stuffing — the automated attack where a password leaked from one site gets tried against hundreds of others, betting you reused it. With 2FA on, that stolen password alone just isn't enough anymore.

sections.title: Turning it on, platform by platform

paragraphs: Start with your Apple ID: Settings → [your name] → Sign-In & Security → Two-Factor Authentication. Then repeat the same search inside each app you use most — email, banking, and social media all have a "Security" or "Two-Factor Authentication" setting in their own account settings.

Start with your Google Account: Settings → Google → Manage your Google Account → Security → 2-Step Verification. Then do the same inside each of your other important apps — the setting is almost always under Settings → Security.

sections.title: Which method to actually pick

bad.label: SMS codes
bad.text: Better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap attacks where someone convinces your carrier to move your number to their phone.

good.label: Authenticator app or security key
good.text: Codes generate on your device itself, with nothing to intercept over the phone network. This is the stronger default whenever a site offers it.

paragraphs: The Toolkit has free authenticator app picks if you don't already have one set up.

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU THINK YOU'VE LOST 2FA ACCESS
warn.text: Most services let you generate backup codes when you first turn on 2FA — save those somewhere offline, not on the same phone. If you're setting up 2FA today, build your 2FA Recovery Kit at the same time so you're never locked out.

checklist: Turned on 2FA for primary email first — it can reset almost everything else
Turned on 2FA for banking and anything holding payment info
Chose an authenticator app or security key over SMS where available
Saved backup codes somewhere offline, not on the phone itself

posts.title: Anatomy of a phishing email, line by line
posts.listDesc: Every part of a phishing email is doing a specific job. Once you know what to look for, most of them fall apart in seconds.
posts.intro: Phishing emails aren't random — every line is built to do a specific job: borrow trust, manufacture urgency, and get you to click before you look too closely. Once you know what each part is actually doing, they stop being convincing.
posts.tldr: Phishing emails combine a spoofed sender name, generic greeting, manufactured urgency, and a link whose real destination doesn't match its text. Check the actual sending address and hover the link before clicking — those two checks catch almost all of them.
posts.statLine: $ context — the sender name you see in your inbox can say literally anything; it's the underlying email address, which most inboxes hide by default, that actually tells you where a message came from.

sections.title: The sender name is not the sender

paragraphs: Anyone can set their display name to "Bank Support" or "Amazon" — that's just a label, not proof. What actually matters is the email address underneath it, which most inboxes hide unless you tap the sender name to expand it.
A real company's email will almost always come from its actual domain (like @amazon.com), not a look-alike (@amaz0n-support.com) or a generic address (@gmail.com).

sections.title: The red flags, one by one

items.text: "Dear Customer" instead of your actual name — real companies you have accounts with usually know it.
"Your account will be suspended in 24 hours" — manufactured pressure to stop you from thinking it through.
The visible link text says one thing, but hovering over it (without clicking) shows a completely different, unrelated web address.
An unexpected invoice, shipping label, or "document" attached that you never asked for.

sections.title: What to do instead of clicking

paragraphs: Don't click the link, and don't open the attachment. If the email claims there's a real problem with an account, open that company's app or type its website address in yourself — if something's genuinely wrong, it'll show up there too, with no risky link required.
If you're ever unsure whether a message is real, that uncertainty is itself the answer: legitimate companies don't rely on manufactured panic to get you to act.

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY CLICKED
warn.text: If you entered a password or payment details on a page you reached from an email link, change that password immediately and check your accounts and statements for anything unfamiliar over the next few days. If you opened an attachment, run a security scan on your device.

checklist: Checks the actual sending email address, not just the display name
Notices generic greetings and manufactured urgency for what they are
Hovers links to check the real destination before ever clicking
Goes to the official app or site directly instead of clicking through

posts.title: How to spot a deepfake in 2026
posts.listDesc: The obvious tells from a few years ago mostly don't work anymore. Here's what actually still catches a fake.
posts.intro: Deepfakes used to be easy to catch — flickering edges, weird blinking, a voice that sounded slightly off. Most of those tells are gone now. The good news: a smaller set of tells still hold up, and they're less about pixels and more about context.
posts.tldr: Old deepfake tells (bad blinking, flickering edges) mostly don't work anymore. What still holds up: checking whether the request itself makes sense, verifying through a second channel, and watching for small physics mistakes like lighting and reflections.
posts.statLine: $ context — deepfake detection researchers now describe the arms race as roughly even: as fast as visual tells get fixed by newer models, new ones take their place, which is why context matters more than appearance now.

sections.title: Why deepfakes are harder to catch now

paragraphs: Early deepfakes struggled with natural blinking, consistent lighting, and lip-sync — those were the classic tells. Newer models have largely fixed all three. Judging a video by "does it look believable" alone is a much weaker test than it used to be.
That's why the more reliable checks have shifted away from appearance and toward context: does this request make sense, and can it be verified some other way?

sections.title: The tells that still work

items.text: Lighting on the face that doesn't quite match the background, or reflections (in glasses, windows) that don't line up with what's on screen.
Hands, ears, and hairlines are still where most models struggle most — look for warping or blurring at the edges of a moving face.
A request for money, credentials, or urgent action is a bigger red flag than any visual glitch — that's the actual goal of most deepfake scams.
You're only being reached one way, with no way offered to confirm through a second channel — a real, urgent request usually survives being double-checked.

sections.title: What to do when you're not sure

paragraphs: Verify through a channel the other person doesn't control — call them back on a number you already have, message a mutual contact, or ask something only the real person would know. A deepfake can mimic a face and voice; it can't answer a question it was never fed.
If it's a public figure or a viral clip, a quick search for the same moment from an official or verified source usually settles it fast — real news breaks in more than one place at once.

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY ACTED ON ONE
warn.text: If you sent money, shared credentials, or made a decision based on a video or call that turns out to have been faked, treat it the same as any other scam: contact your bank if money moved, change any passwords involved, and report it — the earlier, the better.

checklist: Knows old tells like bad blinking mostly don't apply anymore
Checks lighting, reflections, hands, and edges when something feels off
Verifies urgent or unusual requests through a second channel
Cross-checks viral clips against official sources before trusting them
